public abstract class MechanismSim<S extends edu.wpi.first.math.Num,I extends edu.wpi.first.math.Num,O extends edu.wpi.first.math.Num> extends Object
The `MechanismSim` class provides a simulation framework for mechanisms that are driven by one or more motors (e.g., an arm, elevator, wrist, roller). It uses a LinearSystemSim (state-space plant) to evolve the mechanism state in simulation based on the voltage that the motor controller *would* apply, which is retrieved from Phoenix 6's simulated TalonFX via getSimState().getMotorVoltage().

Why this exists

In simulation, there is no real encoder. CTRE’s simulated firmware will still compute an output duty cycle/voltage from your control requests (PercentOutput, Voltage, Position/Velocity closed-loop, Motion Magic, etc.). However, the controller needs sensor feedback to close the loop. This class:
  1. Reads the controller’s commanded voltage (what it would put on the motor terminals).
  2. Feeds that into a physics model (LinearSystemSim) to integrate position/velocity.
  3. Writes the simulated rotor position/velocity back to the Talon via setRawRotorPosition(...) and setRotorVelocity(...).

Units & conventions

  • Voltages: Volts (V). The supply voltage is taken from RobotController.getBatteryVoltage() and pushed into the Talon sim.
  • Rotor signals: The setters setRawRotorPosition and setRotorVelocity are in rotor units (rotations, rotations-per-second). If you configured FeedbackConfigs.withSensorToMechanismRatio(G), you must convert your mechanism state into rotor units before writing these values.
  • Mechanism state: Your subclass decides whether to maintain state in mechanism units and convert, or track rotor units directly. See getSimulatedRotorPositionRotations() and getSimulatedRotorVelocityRPS().

Timing model

A Notifier ticks this sim at a fixed period (default 5 ms = 200 Hz). Faster rates are more stable and realistic for closed-loop control, but use more CPU. You can tweak the period via the call to startPeriodic(...) in the constructor.

Followers

Any follower Talons supplied in followerIOs will receive the same simulated rotor position/velocity as the master. This mirrors typical FRC usage where followers share the same sensor/shaft state.

Subclassing

Implement getSimulatedRotorPositionRotations() and getSimulatedRotorVelocityRPS() to return the current rotor position/velocity derived from your plant.
  • If your plant tracks mechanism angle/speed, multiply by sensorPerMechanismRatio (i.e., gear ratio) to convert to rotor units.

Threading

The Notifier runs on its own real-time thread. Do not block in updateSimState(). Keep state shared between threads either atomic or confined; this class uses AtomicReference for the last-computed values. If you log or access additional shared state, use appropriate concurrency hygiene.

Key Phoenix 6 interactions

  • simState.getMotorVoltage() is the commanded terminal voltage from Phoenix’s internal loop (duty × bus V, or the result of PID in closed-loop modes).
  • setRawRotorPosition(...) and setRotorVelocity(...) feed the Talon’s simulated encoder.
  • Setting simState.setSupplyVoltage(busV) lets the Talon scale duty-cycle to volts realistically.

  • Method Details

    • addFriction

      protected double addFriction(double motorVoltage, double frictionVoltage)
      Applies a simple Coulomb-like friction deadband to the motor terminal voltage. If the absolute voltage is below frictionVoltage, returns zero. Otherwise, subtracts (or adds) the friction voltage in the sign direction.

      Note: This is an optional helper; currently disabled in updateSimState(). You can re-enable by wrapping the read voltage with this method.

      Parameters:
      motorVoltage - The commanded motor terminal voltage (V).
      frictionVoltage - The effective friction drop (V) to model static friction/Coulomb losses.
      Returns:
      Adjusted motor voltage (V) after friction.

    • updateSimState

      protected void updateSimState()
      Core simulation loop. Called periodically by the Notifier.
      1. Push current battery voltage to Talon sim via setSupplyVoltage so Phoenix can scale duty→volts.
      2. Read Phoenix’s commanded voltage via getMotorVoltage().
      3. Optionally invert/sign-adjust and apply to the plant input.
      4. Integrate plant by dt seconds.
      5. Compute rotor position/velocity and write them to the Talon sim's sensor.
      6. Mirror rotor signals to all follower Talons.

      Threading: Avoid heavy work here; keep it deterministic and fast.
